extracted.intended_audience: IRB members, research ethicists, regulators, and legal/academic scholars interested in human subjects research governance
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) should assess the reasonableness of research risk–benefit profiles, including competing interpretations (social welfare maximization, participant welfare maximization, proportionality), what risks and benefits to count, and empirical/administrative responses and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness as Cost–Benefit Analysis / Social Welfare Maximization
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreting risk–benefit reasonableness as cost–benefit analysis (CBA) would mean research is “reasonable” whenever expected benefits to society and to participants outweigh risks to participants; IRBs would choose the alternative that maximizes net social welfare regardless of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If implemented, this construction would aggregate risks to participants on one side and expected benefits (to participants and society) on the other and direct IRBs to pick the option that maximizes aggregate welfare; criticism: would ignore distributional effects and could conscript individuals into research despite unequal distribution of costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: HSR risk–benefit analysis is not standard CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Human subjects research (HSR) risk–benefit analysis is not intended to be a plenary, utilitarian CBA; instead HSR regulations direct IRBs to consider immediate risks to participants, benefits to participants (if any), and benefits to society in the form of knowledge production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory construction directs IRBs to ignore costs to any party other than participants, long-term risks to participants from policy implications of knowledge gained, and benefits to nonparticipants (e.g., academic freedom, employment). Thus IRB analysis is narrower than standard welfare-maximizing CBA (see 45 C.F.R. § 46.111(a)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness as Participant Welfare Maximization (Best-Interests Standard / Equipoise)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative interpretation is that research is “reasonable” only when enrollment is expected to be in the participant’s best interests—i.e., to maximize her welfare relative to her alternatives (a fiduciary or best-interests standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (often tied to notions of equipoise in clinical research) would render acceptable only relatively rare therapeutic research and would preclude altruistic participation; thus it is implausible as a general regulatory interpretation because it makes typical HSR unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity in risk–benefit tradeoff preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective participants are heterogeneous in how they trade off risks and benefits (how much benefit, and the mix of personal vs societal benefit, is required before risks are acceptable), and IRBs cannot access or implement individualized determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reasonableness is perspectival (to whom must it be reasonable?), IRBs face a problem: individuals will reasonably disagree, and IRBs must make a single determination binding on all; empirical studies (e.g., differences among patients, clinicians, and public; variation in IRB decisions) illustrate this heterogeneity and its consequences for inconsistent approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory phrasing: 'reasonable' / 'proportionate' / 'favorable' / 'justified' standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary regulations and ethical guidelines characterize acceptable risk–benefit relationships using terms like “reasonable,” “proportionate,” “favorable,” or “justified.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrasing sets no explicit cap on the magnitude of risk nonvulnerable participants may assume; in theory very large risks could be deemed reasonable if the study has great social promise, which raises distributional and heterogeneity concerns when IRBs make determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical standard: benefits must outweigh risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier regulatory schemes (and many historical ethical codes) required that risks to subjects be outweighed by the sum of benefit to the subject and the importance of the knowledge to be gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HHS’s earlier regulations and codes like Helsinki/Nuremberg held a benefits-outweigh-risks rule; the modern shift to a vaguer “reasonableness” standard replaced that stricter test, altering how IRBs evaluate protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of risks IRBs must consider (breadth of risk types)
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs are directed to consider risks of virtually every nature — physical, psychological, social, economic, legal, and de minimis harms (e.g., discomfort, inconvenience, boredom) — posed by any aspect of the research protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All elements of the protocol should be subjected to risk analysis (NY State guidance); examples include shortness of breath, anxiety, time spent traveling, disruption of routine, embarrassment. The only category IRBs are directed to ignore are possible long-range effects of applying knowledge gained (e.g., public policy effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eggshell participant / conservative risk estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs tend to evaluate protocols as if the risk faced by the most vulnerable or ‘eggshell’ prospective participant were the risk faced by all or the modal participant, often without relying on population frequency data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs frequently speculate about likelihood and magnitude of harms and thus treat rare harms seriously; empirical evidence shows IRBs approve/reject differently, suggesting overcaution driven by focusing on conceivable rather than probable harms, with attendant costs to research and knowledge production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory exclusion of long-range effects from IRB calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs are directed not to consider the possible long-range effects of applying knowledge gained in the research (for example, effects on public policy) when conducting risk–benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified in regulation (45 C.F.R. § 46.111(a)(2)); limits scope of benefits/costs IRBs may weigh and narrows HSR risk–benefit analysis to more immediate/participant-focused concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'benefit' (IRB Guidebook) versus narrower agency practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRB Guidebook defines 'benefit' broadly as any 'valued or desired outcome; an advantage,' but other agency guidance and canonical norms effectively instruct IRBs not to count many outcomes participants value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the broad Guidebook definition, IRBs are commonly directed (and practice) to count primarily direct medical benefits to participants and societal knowledge; the NY guidelines explicitly note that altruistic satisfaction and financial compensation are not the type of 'benefit' IRBs should consider in evaluating risk–benefit ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of altruism, warm-glow, and intangible participant benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs do not count participants’ preferences for 'pure' altruism, warm-glow utility, curiosity, empowerment, or other intangible benefits in their risk–benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible rationales include avoiding double-counting societal benefits; nevertheless IRB practice systematically ignores these motivating benefits despite their empirical importance to participant decisionmaking, contributing to an impoverished view of human benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of payment or remuneration as a benefit (and concern about undue inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct payments or other forms of remuneration offered as incentive or reward should not be considered a 'benefit' to be gained from research (per OHRP IRB Guidebook); payments are often treated as potential undue inducements or coercive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment in money or in-kind (e.g., course credit) is typically excluded from the benefit side of IRB analysis; IRBs have sometimes reduced or prohibited payments (example: reducing undergraduate payment from $25 to $10), and consider healthy volunteers in Phase I trials vulnerable to undue inducement because of payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment in kind (extra credit, nonmonetary benefits) treated as non-benefit / potentially coercive
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonmonetary payments (e.g., extra course credit) are not counted as benefits and are often judged to be coercive or unduly influential on certain populations (e.g., students).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRB Guidebook notes controversy over requiring participation for course credit and suggests mechanisms to diminish coercion; IRBs frequently express concern that such offers are the 'offer they can't refuse.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical benefits are often downplayed or undercounted
rubrics_metrics.description: The category of participant medical benefit is often conservatively assessed or downweighted by IRBs, sometimes to the point of rating a 'zero' on the utility scale, in part to avoid therapeutic misconception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs and ethicists claim low probability of benefit in many Phase I trials (e.g., oncology), yet aggregate data can conceal important variation (some compounds have substantial response rates; historic and recent successes like cisplatin and imatinib demonstrate possible substantial clinical benefits). This conservative stance affects whether trials are judged 'reasonable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipoise requirements for randomized controlled trials (RCTs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional wisdom holds that RCTs are acceptable only if the relevant expert community is in 'equipoise'—i.e., indifferent between treatments (internal equipoise) and indentation that enrollment is not inferior to alternatives (external equipoise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equipoise is used to ensure RCTs do not convert research into quasi-therapy or violate fiduciary obligations; key references include Fried (coining 'equipoise') and Freedman ('clinical equipoise'); tensions exist between equipoise, the Belmont view of volunteers, and obligations of investigators.
